The core insight is that while blind and sighted individuals share analogous perceptual contents such as 'big/little' and 'near/far', their underlying spatial metrics differ fundamentally. The tactile space S_t encodes constant physical dimensions, whereas visual space S_v encodes apparent size and distance through perspective. This leads to a dual structure where the same conceptual content maps differently under each modality. The divergence manifests in the inability to translate tactile names into visual recognition, indicating a breakdown in cross-modal isomorphism. The failure mode arises from the mismatch between tactile and visual metric tensors, causing a breakdown in perceptual alignment. This is mathematically modeled as a non-isometric embedding of perceptual manifolds, where the intrinsic geometry of one modality cannot be directly mapped to another without additional transformation.
